title: Backup and Disaster Recovery
seoTitle: Backup and Disaster Recovery for Small Businesses
seoDescription: What backup and disaster recovery mean for business software, RPO and RTO in plain words, the 3-2-1 rule, and how to test that restores work.
summary: Backup is keeping copies of your data; disaster recovery is the plan and practice for getting systems working again after a failure, attack or mistake. For a business, the real test is not whether backups exist but whether you can restore them quickly and completely.

dataPoints.label: Two key numbers
dataPoints.value: RPO: how much data you can afford to lose. RTO: how long you can afford to be down

dataPoints.label: 3-2-1 rule
dataPoints.value: Three copies, on two different types of storage, one kept off-site or in a separate account

dataPoints.label: Biggest threat today
dataPoints.value: Ransomware that also encrypts reachable backups

dataPoints.label: Most common failure
dataPoints.value: Backups never test-restored until the day they are needed

body:
## A sensible baseline for SMEs

| Item | Baseline |
| --- | --- |
| Database backups | Automatic daily, with point-in-time recovery if available |
| Copies | At least one in a separate cloud account or region |
| Retention | 30 days or more |
| Restore test | Quarterly, timed and written down |
| Access | Backups not deletable from everyday admin accounts |

Ask any software vendor how backups work and request a restore demonstration. See [cloud hosting](/glossary/cloud-hosting) and [data migration](/glossary/data-migration).

faqs.q: Does cloud hosting mean we are backed up?
faqs.a: Not automatically. Check what the provider backs up, for how long, and who can restore it.

faqs.q: How often should we test restores?
faqs.a: At least quarterly, and after any major change to the system.
